title: Lula trailed after round one in Brazil, then won the runoff by 4.4 million votes
body: Brazil elects its president in two rounds. A candidate with more than half of the valid votes (blank and null ballots don’t count) wins outright; otherwise the top two meet again on the last Sunday of October. On 4 October 2026, with 12 candidates, Flávio Bolsonaro led with 47.03% and Lula had 45.16%. On 25 October Lula won the runoff with 51.79%, by [64,256,232 votes to 59,826,041](https://ndmais.com.br/politica/quantos-votos-lula-e-flavio-bolsonaro-tiveram-em-2026/), according to the electoral court (TSE). Between the rounds he gained 10.4 million votes and his rival 3.7 million: more than the 9.3 million won by the ten other candidates, because the runoff also had 4.8 million more valid votes. [Reuters](https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/brazil-heads-polls-runoff-between-070736480.html) reported that he is the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy to be elected after finishing second in round one; Flávio Bolsonaro said he would seek to have the result annulled over a court ruling that extended voting by two hours. Voting is compulsory for literate citizens aged 18 to 69, and the new four-year term starts on 5 January 2027.

slides.question: Lula trailed by 2.2 million votes after round one. What share of the other candidates’ 9.3 million votes did he need?
slides.explanation: About 62%, if everyone else voted as before: he needed 2.2 million more of those votes than his rival. In the end the runoff also brought 4.8 million more valid votes.

slides.alt: Animation on white with sweeping curves: an electronic voting machine, then round-one bars, Flávio Bolsonaro 47.0% and Lula 45.2%, under a 50% line. The others’ 9.3 million votes become squares split between the two, then runoff bars grow to 51.79% for Lula, and a calendar shows 5 January 2027.

slides.prompt: Split the free votes between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro. Find a split, with or without new voters, that lets the second-placed candidate win.
slides.takeaway: With no new voters Lula needs 62% of the others’ votes. In the real runoff he gained 10.4 of the 14.1 million votes added between the rounds, about 74%, and won with 51.79%.

slides.heading: Votes for the two finalists, in millions
Why two rounds?
slides.text: A runoff makes sure the president is backed by a majority of the valid votes, not just the largest minority. With 12 names on the ballot in round one, the leader had 47%. In the runoff only two are left, so one of them must pass 50%, and voters whose candidate is out get a second say.

slides.question: Which ballots are left out when Brazil checks whether a candidate has more than half of the votes?
slides.explanation: Brazil’s constitution counts only valid votes: a candidate needs an absolute majority of them, not counting blank and null ballots.
